pos: n. (proper name; a man of Moresheth — the designation of Micah the prophet)
etymology: Hebrew Morashti, the gentilic of Moresheth-gath, a town in the lowlands of Judah named at Micah 1:14.
biblical_def: The word occurs twice, and both times it identifies the prophet: “The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Micah 1:1). A century later the elders of Judah cited him by the same title to save Jeremiah's life: “Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah... Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps” (Jeremiah 26:18). Their argument was precedent — Hezekiah did not put Micah to death for saying it, and Judah should not put Jeremiah to death now (Jeremiah 26:19). The Authorized Version uses Morasthite in these two verses alone. The dictionary notes that Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12 almost exactly, which is a remarkable internal witness: the elders of a later generation could quote a written prophet by name, by reign, and by text, and the text they quoted is the one we have. Scripture cites Scripture as Scripture, and a country prophet from a lowland village was still being quoted in the city a hundred years on.

corruption_summary: Micah is commonly divided among several authors and centuries; Jeremiah 26:18 names one Micah of Moresheth and quotes him.
corruption_paragraphs: The critical treatment of Micah splits the book between an eighth-century prophet and later hands, assigning the hopeful oracles to post-exilic editors. Jeremiah 26:18 is evidence against the method: a hundred years after Micah, the elders of Judah knew the man, his town, his reign, and his words, and quoted chapter 3 verbatim. The dictionary holds one Micah of Moresheth and the integrity of the book that bears his name.

The principle to recover is the authority of a written prophet. The elders did not appeal to tradition or to feeling; they appealed to a text and to what a godly king had done about it. Scripture was already functioning as Scripture inside the Old Testament.

pos: n. pl. (proper name; one of the two families of the Levitical house of Merari)
etymology: Hebrew Mushi, the gentilic of Mushi, the second son of Merari; Merari was the third son of Levi.
biblical_def: The Mushites appear twice, in the two Levitical musters: “Of Merari was the family of the Mahlites, and the family of the Mushites: these are the families of Merari” (Numbers 3:33), and in the later list at Numbers 26:58. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes the duty attached to the house. Levi had three sons, and each house had its charge about the tabernacle: Gershon the curtains, Kohath the ark and the holy vessels, Merari the boards, bars, pillars, and sockets. “These shall pitch on the side of the tabernacle northward” (Numbers 3:35). The Mushites carried the frame — the heavy timber and the bronze bases on which the whole structure stood. Nobody saw their work once the tabernacle was up; the boards were covered and the sockets were in the ground. And the assignment was not theirs to choose: the house of Merari was given the boards by the word of the LORD through Moses, and carried them through forty years of wilderness. God assigns the post, the post is unseen, and the tent does not stand without it.

corruption_paragraphs: The Levitical assignments are sometimes read as a priestly caste system invented to secure privilege. The content of the assignments argues otherwise: the house of Merari was given the heaviest and least visible load in the camp, and the charge was laid on them by name, by family, and by the word of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints the post and the post is not chosen. The Mushites carried sockets of brass for forty years, and the tabernacle of the LORD stood on them. The body of Christ is ordered the same way, and the apostle says the members which seem to be more feeble are necessary.

pos: n. (proper name; two ancestors of the Lord Jesus in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Melchi, from Hebrew melek, king — the same root as Melchizedek, king of righteousness, and Malchiah.
biblical_def: The name occurs twice in one chapter, of two men in the same line: “Which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi, which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Janna, which was the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:24), and twenty-six generations further back, “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam” (Luke 3:28). The Authorized Version uses the name twice and nowhere else. The dictionary notes the genealogy both verses belong to. Luke traces the line backwards from Joseph to Heli, through David's son Nathan rather than Solomon, and back past Abraham to Adam, which was the son of God. Matthew traces forward from Abraham through Solomon to Joseph. The two lists serve two purposes: Matthew gives the legal royal title through Joseph, Luke the descent of the Lord's humanity. Luke is careful at the outset to say Joseph was the supposed father (Luke 3:23), because the virgin birth stands behind the whole list. The name Melchi means my king, and it stands twice in the ancestry of the King.

corruption_summary: The two genealogies are commonly offered as a contradiction at the front of the New Testament; they are two lines serving two purposes.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard objection is that Matthew and Luke give irreconcilable ancestries for one man. They give different lines because they are doing different things: Matthew establishes legal title to David's throne through Joseph and through Solomon, and Luke gives the descent of the Lord's humanity through Nathan. The old explanations — Luke's list through Mary, or a levirate marriage behind Heli and Jacob — are both consistent with the texts, and neither evangelist is in difficulty.

The principle to recover is Luke 3:23. The parenthesis as was supposed is deliberate: Luke, who opened his Gospel with the annunciation and Mary's question how shall this be, writes the genealogy knowing Joseph was not the father. The virgin birth is not an awkwardness in the list; it is the reason the list is phrased that way.

pos: n. (proper name; two ancestors of the Lord Jesus in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Matthat, a shortened form of the Hebrew Mattithiah, gift of Jehovah — the same element behind Matthew, Mattaniah, and Nathanael.
biblical_def: Matthat occurs twice, of two men in Luke's line: “Which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi, which was the son of Melchi” (Luke 3:24), and later, “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29). The Authorized Version uses the name twice, and in both places it is followed immediately by a Levi — the same pairing of names twice in one genealogy, which is what families do. The dictionary notes the meaning, since there is no biography to note. Matthat is gift of Jehovah, contracted from Mattithiah; the same thought stands in Matthew, in Mattaniah, in Nathanael, in Theodore. Among the seventy-odd names of Luke 3 there are several that confess the LORD in their syllables — Melchi my king, Matthat gift of Jehovah, Mattatha, Elmodam, Eliezer God is help. Generations of obscure Judeans named their sons after the God of Israel, century after century, with no idea what their line was carrying. The genealogy of the Lord Jesus is largely a list of men whose only recorded act was to beget the next one.

corruption_paragraphs: The one reading to resist treats the long genealogies as padding to be skipped. Luke wrote seventy-seven names under inspiration and ended them at Adam, which was the son of God — a deliberate claim that the Lord Jesus is kinsman to the whole race and not to Israel only, which is what Luke's Gospel is about from Simeon's song onward.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the worth of the unrecorded generation. Matthat's one act in the Bible is to have had a son, and that is enough to put him in the ancestry of Christ. Ordinary faithfulness, repeated across centuries by men nobody remembers, is the ordinary material of God's purposes.

pos: n. (proper name; grandfather of Joseph the husband of Mary, in Matthew's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Matthan, from Hebrew mattan, a gift. A distinct name from Matthat of Luke 3, though built on the same root.
biblical_def: Matthan stands two generations from the end of Matthew's genealogy: “And Eliud begat Eleazar; and Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob” (Matthew 1:15), and then “Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ” (Matthew 1:16). The Authorized Version uses the name twice in that one verse. The dictionary notes the construction of Matthew 1:16, which is the most carefully built sentence in the chapter. Every link before it reads begat: Eleazar begat Matthan, Matthan begat Jacob, Jacob begat Joseph. Then the chain breaks. It does not say Joseph begat Jesus. It says Joseph was the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus — the relative pronoun is feminine and refers to Mary alone. Matthew has traced forty-one generations of fathers begetting sons in order to arrive at a birth that had no father. The genealogy establishes the legal royal line through Joseph, and in its last clause denies the natural descent, which is precisely the double thing the Messiah had to be: the legal heir of David's throne, and conceived of the Holy Ghost.

corruption_summary: Matthew's genealogy is read as a late construction; its final clause is a precise doctrinal statement guarding the virgin birth.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments of Matthew 1 explain the list as theological artifice: three symmetrical sets of fourteen, assembled to make a point. The symmetry is real and Matthew names it himself in verse 17 — an inspired writer is allowed to arrange his material. What the list is not is careless. The break in the begat chain at verse 16 is deliberate and exact.

The principle to recover is what that break secures. Joseph gives the Lord Jesus His legal descent from David and so His title to the throne; Mary gives Him His humanity; and no man gives Him His person, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. Deny the virgin birth and Matthew 1:16 has to be rewritten.

pos: n. (proper name; wife of Hadar, the last of the kings of Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Mehetab'el, meaning God does good, or whom God benefits — from yatab, to do good, and El, God.
biblical_def: Mehetabel is named twice, in the two copies of the list of Edom's kings: “And Baalhanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Pau; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab” (Genesis 36:39), with 1 Chronicles 1:50. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes where the list sits and what it is for. Genesis 36:31 introduces it: “And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel.” Esau's line had kings while Jacob's line had none. Eight kings of Edom are named, with their cities and, for the last, his wife and her mother and her grandmother — three generations of women in one verse. The point of the chapter is the patience of promise. Esau prospered first and visibly; Israel waited, and the sceptre came to Judah in God's time. A woman whose name means God does good was queen in Edom while the children of promise had no king at all.

That inference is not required: the promise of kings to Abraham and Jacob was already given (Genesis 17:6; 35:11), and a writer who knew the promise could note that Edom got there first. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship.

pos: n. (proper name; grandparent of Mehetabel, wife of the last king of Edom)
etymology: Hebrew Mey-zahab, literally waters of gold — from mayim, waters, and zahab, gold.
biblical_def: Mezahab is named twice, both times at the third remove: “his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab” (Genesis 36:39), with 1 Chronicles 1:50. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. Nothing else is recorded — not the sex of the bearer, not a city, not a deed. The dictionary notes the name itself, which is one of the most striking in Scripture: waters of gold. Hebrew names are frequently sentences or pictures, and this one is a picture of what Edom was, a trading kingdom on the caravan road with gold enough to name a child after. Three generations of a royal Edomite family are recorded in one clause of Genesis 36, and the furthest back is Waters of Gold. The chapter's subject is the line of Esau, who sold a birthright for a meal and received in exchange a prosperous kingdom with eight kings and no promise. The dictionary sets the name beside the verdict Scripture gives on Edom: “Esau have I hated” (Romans 9:13), not for want of gold, and “I have made thee small among the heathen” (Obadiah 1:2). Waters of gold run out.

corruption_summary: Romans 9:13 is softened into a statement about nations or about relative preference; Scripture states unconditional election and the dictionary holds it.
corruption_paragraphs: Every scheme that makes election depend on foreseen faith must do something with Romans 9:13. The common expedients are to make the hatred mere lesser-love, or to confine the statement to the nations of Israel and Edom rather than the men. Paul forecloses both: he argues from the twins before birth, before either had done good or evil, and draws the conclusion that it is not of him that willeth nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.

The principle to recover is unconditional election, as the 1689 Confession states it: God's decree is according to His good pleasure, not according to anything foreseen in the creature. Esau's line had kings, cities, and a grandmother named Waters of Gold; Jacob's line had a promise. Obadiah 1:2 records which lasted.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of the house of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Sismay, of uncertain meaning. The name occurs twice, both in a single verse.
biblical_def: Sisamai is one link in a four-generation chain: “And Eleasah begat Sisamai, and Sisamai begat Shallum” (1 Chronicles 2:40), and the chain continues, “And Shallum begat Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begat Elishama” (1 Chronicles 2:41). The Authorized Version uses the name twice, both within the one verse, and nothing else is said of him. The dictionary notes what the passage is. 1 Chronicles 2 is the genealogy of Judah, written for a people just returned from Babylon who needed to know who they were — which families held which fields, which house was royal, which was priestly. The Chronicler works through Judah's sons, then Hezron, then Jerahmeel and Caleb, naming men nobody had heard of since before the exile. The purpose is restoration. A nation that has been deported for seventy years and comes home has to be able to prove its descent, and the register is how it does so. Sisamai is in the Bible because a returning Judahite needed to show his line, and God saw to it that the line was written down before the city fell.

A written descent was a legal necessity for a restored people, and the Chronicler supplied it.

The registers were written while the kingdom still stood; they were needed seventy years later by men who had been born in Babylon. He prepares the record before the exile that makes it necessary.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite head of a father's house dwelling in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Shashaq, of uncertain meaning, possibly from a root for longing or for running.
biblical_def: Shashak is named twice, in the Benjamite genealogy: “And Ahio, Shashak, and Jeremoth” (1 Chronicles 8:14), and then at the head of his own household, “And Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak” (1 Chronicles 8:25). The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The chapter summarises the men of his class in one sentence: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). The dictionary notes the oddity of the chapter he stands in. 1 Chronicles 8 is a Benjamite register, and five verses after Shashak's sons it gives the line that matters most in the tribe: “And Ner begat Kish, and Kish begat Saul, and Saul begat Jonathan, and Malchishua, and Abinadab, and Eshbaal” (1 Chronicles 8:33). The Chronicler, writing the history of the house of David, takes a whole chapter to register the tribe of the king David displaced, and traces Saul's descendants for twelve further generations. That is not the behaviour of a partisan document. Benjamin kept its place in the record, its heads of houses in Jerusalem, and its deposed royal line in full.

corruption_paragraphs: Chronicles is often described as a partisan rewriting of history in David's favour, with inconvenient material removed. The Benjamite chapter is awkward for that thesis: the Chronicler registers Saul's tribe at length, names Saul's sons, and carries his descendants down twelve generations past the fall of his house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour of the ordinary household head. Shashak is named, his two sons are named, and the chapter calls such men chief men who dwelt in Jerusalem. Scripture records the men who kept houses in the holy city, not only the men who sat on thrones.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the six sons of Azel, a descendant of Saul)
etymology: Hebrew She'aryah, probably meaning Jehovah esteems, or the LORD has regard — or, on another reading, from she'ar, a remnant.
biblical_def: Sheariah is named twice, in the two copies of one verse: “And Azel had six sons, whose names are these, Azrikam, Bocheru, and Ishmael, and Sheariah, and Obadiah, and Hanan. All these were the sons of Azel” (1 Chronicles 8:38), repeated at 1 Chronicles 9:44. The Authorized Version uses the name twice. The dictionary notes whose family this is. Azel stands at the end of the long descent of Saul — Ner begat Kish, Kish begat Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33), and twelve generations later Azel has six sons, of whom Sheariah is the fourth. The house of Saul lost the throne, lost its heir at Gilboa, lost seven of its men to the Gibeonites, and is still being registered name by name four hundred years on. If the name is from she'ar, it means remnant, which would be exact: Sheariah is a remnant of a fallen royal house, listed in the chronicle of the house that replaced it. Scripture has a steady habit of this. God does not erase the names of those He has set aside, and the last Benjamite to be famous in the Bible is the apostle Paul.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one reading to correct supposes that God's rejection of Saul's dynasty was a rejection of Saul's tribe. It was not. Benjamin stayed with Judah at the division of the kingdom, supplied men to David's thirty, held heads of houses in Jerusalem, and produced the apostle to the Gentiles.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Romans 11:1. Hath God cast away his people? God forbid — and the man who asks the question names himself of the tribe of Benjamin. A house set aside from the throne is not a house cast off from mercy.
